name: Nano titanium dioxide

lead: Nano titanium dioxide is a very fine mineral powder used in sunscreens to absorb and scatter UV light. Its small particles make mineral sunscreens look sheerer than older, chalky formulas.
It is often paired with ultrafine zinc oxide. Interest in it comes from people who prefer mineral over organic filters, while its nanoparticle form is also the subject of safety discussion.

paras: As a wide-bandgap semiconductor it absorbs UV below about 400 nm and scatters little visible light at nanoscale sizes. Under UV it can also generate reactive oxygen species, which is the basis of its photocatalytic uses.

IARC classifies inhaled TiO2 dust as Group 2B and advises against sprayable sunscreens. Laboratory studies report gut-barrier and ecological effects at tested exposures. The EU banned it as a food additive in 2022; sunscreen use is regulated separately and no sunscreen-specific clinical trials were found.

lead: Nano titanium dioxide (nano-TiO2) refers to engineered particles of titanium dioxide, typically 1 to 100 nanometres across, that absorb ultraviolet light while remaining largely transparent in visible light.[1] In sunscreens they are used as a mineral UV filter, often alongside ultrafine zinc oxide, to reduce sunburn and long-term sun damage.[2] The smaller particle size is the reason such formulations can look sheer on the skin rather than leaving the opaque white cast associated with older mineral products.[1]

Nanoscale TiO2 also appears in paints, plastics, food colouring, self-cleaning coatings and biomedical research.[1][3] Its safety has been reviewed for several exposure routes. A 2010 review addressed "nano" titanium dioxide and zinc oxide in sunscreens specifically,[4] and a 2016 review compared toxicity by route of exposure.[5] Regulators have treated inhaled dust and food-additive use differently from topical use.[2]
infobox: Inorganic mineral UV filter (nanoparticle form of TiO2)
UV absorber / scatterer in mineral sunscreens[2]

paras: Ultrafine titanium dioxide is used in sunscreens, frequently combined with ultrafine zinc oxide.[2] Because it is a wide-bandgap semiconductor, it absorbs UV wavelengths below roughly 400 nm, and nanoscale particles scatter less visible light than larger pigment-grade particles, which allows clearer formulations.[1] Some sunscreens add iron oxide pigments for additional protection against visible light.[2]
Mineral filters of this kind are described by proponents as an alternative to organic (chemical) filters. This article does not compare them; see the entries for individual filters.

TiO2 nanoparticles are chemically stable and poorly soluble in water.[1] When struck by UV light, they can generate reactive oxygen species such as hydroxyl radicals; this photocatalytic behaviour underlies applications in self-cleaning surfaces and pollutant degradation, and is also the reason nanoparticle coatings and surface treatments are studied in toxicology.[1][2] The photocatalytic property was reported by Akira Fujishima in 1967 and published in 1972 (the Honda-Fujishima effect).[2]
Particle properties such as surface area, primary size and crystal phase influence how the particles disperse in liquids, which in turn affects toxicity testing.[6]

The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies inhaled TiO2 dust as Group 2B, "possibly carcinogenic to humans", and advises against sprayable sunscreens because of inhalation risk.[2] Wikipedia notes it is not known how well healthy skin blocks TiO2 or whether damaged skin or prolonged use changes exposure, and that sunscreen on injured skin or open wounds is not recommended.[2]

Laboratory studies have reported that TiO2 nanoparticles can cross gut epithelium in ex vivo and in vivo models and alter its permeability,[7] and toxicity in aquatic organisms such as mussels and Daphnia has been examined.[8][9] Grokipedia summarises literature linking high-dose or direct cellular exposure to oxidative stress and inflammation, while noting that some weight-of-evidence reviews attribute many findings to cytotoxicity rather than nanoparticle-specific genotoxicity.[1]

In food, the European Food Safety Authority concluded in 2021 that genotoxicity could not be ruled out, and the EU withdrew authorisation of TiO2 (E171) as a food additive from 7 February 2022; the UK and Health Canada did not follow, and the US permits it up to 1% of a food by weight.[2] These actions concern ingestion, not sunscreen use.

No studies found of nano-TiO2 sunscreens as an appearance or skin-protection product in the sources reviewed for this article. Registered trials that mention titanium dioxide nanoparticles concern dental products such as denture materials, a bleaching gel and a mouthwash, which are different uses.[10] Safety evidence for sunscreen use comes mainly from review articles and laboratory work.[4][5]

timeline.event: TiO2 first mass-produced as a white pigment.[2]
